Section One: Iconography. Section Two: Translation, Volume One. Section Three: Translation, Volume Two.
Exegesis on the Third [Chapter], Part Three;
Cultivation of Contemplation, Part Four;
Relinquishing the Body, Part Five.

Copying (Eighth) Tenth Scroll 1: Images Image No. 1:

A Golden Image of the Buddha Preaching the Sūtra in the Western Regions; An Image of the Buddha Preaching this Sūtra at Vulture Peak in the Western Regions; [Compiled by] Shi [Daoxuan] of the Song Dynasty.

Huihao created a painting of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; Emperor Taizu of the Later Wei created a painting of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; Lady Yin of the Jin dynasty created a Dharma Flower Terrace; Consort Xie of the Song dynasty created Fahua Temple;

Zheng Qiong, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices of the Later Wei, created a Dharma Flower Hall; Śramaṇa Huili of the Jin dynasty created a Prabhūtaratna Stūpa; Liu Fuai of the Song dynasty created Duobao Temple and a Prabhūtaratna Stūpa;

Xu Yan, Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Qi dynasty, created a stone Prabhūtaratna Stūpa; and Śramaṇa Facheng of Wuzhen Temple in the Tang dynasty created a Prabhūtaratna Stūpa, a Dharma Flower Stūpa, as well as a Dharma Flower [Hall].

In the Sui dynasty, Xiao Jing, the Director of the National Academy (Guozijiu), constructed a Many-Jeweled Stūpa (Duobao Ta). In the Song dynasty, Empress Dowager Luzhao commissioned an image of Samantabhadra. In the Song dynasty, the monk Daojiong performed the Samantabhadra fast (Puxian zhai). In the Song dynasty, the monk Sengbao also performed the Samantabhadra fast.
According to the *Jiwen tu* (Diagram of the Jetavana Monastery): [The text continues with the description of the monastery layout.]
On the upper story of the eastern pavilion of the former Buddha hall,
there is a silver image;
within the image is a seven-jeweled tower-palace.
Within the pavilion, there is a jeweled pond with precious flowers.
Upon the flowers are white jade images.
Within the lotuses in the pond—
There was a silver stūpa;
within the heart of that stūpa,
there was a pearl stūpa.
Within the stupa are the two images of Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna.
Regarding those who preach the seventh assembly of the Lotus Sūtra,
it is further said:
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is in substance identical to the *Avataṃsaka*;
it was expounded across many assemblies of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
That which is translated now corresponds to the third assembly.
Furthermore, it is said:
The multi-storied palace has four terraces and five tiers;
on the uppermost level is a vaimanī jewel.
This jewel...
The Buddhas of the past once preached the Lotus Sūtra therein,
three times transforming the pure land.
Everything contained within the sūtras is fully manifested therein;
this is according to the records transmitted in the Western Regions.
To the south of the Ganges River in the kingdom of Magadha in Central India, there is an old city.
It is more than seventy li in circuit and has been desolate for many years.
The foundations still remain.
In the past, when human lifespans were immeasurable years,
this was called the city of Kusumapura.
In the language of Tang, it is called the City of Fragrant Flower Palaces;
when the human lifespan reached several thousand years,
it was renamed the City of Pāṭaliputra.
This is the city of Pāṭaliputra.
Over four hundred li to the southwest of this city,
one crosses the Nairañjanā River.
He arrived at the city of Gayā.
Twenty-odd *li* to the southwest of the city,
he reached the Bodhi tree.
At the Vajrāsana and other sites,
to the east of the Bodhi tree,
he crossed a great river and entered a vast forest wilderness.
After traveling more than one hundred *li*,
he arrived at Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
More than one hundred *li* to the northeast of Mount Kukkuṭapāda, there was...
Reaching the Great Mountain,
he entered it and traveled eastward for over sixty li until he arrived at the city of Upper Maogong.
This city is precisely the center of the kingdom of Magadha;
it was the capital of former kings and produces much fragrant *kuśa* grass.
Therefore, it was named accordingly.
A lofty mountain encircles it on all four sides,
serving as its outer wall.
It communicates to the west via a narrow path;
the mountain gate opens to the north.
Its circumference is over one hundred and fifty li.
The trees flourished in spring,
all turning the color of gold.
Formerly, King Bimbisāra...
In this capital city,
the common people registered as householders have repeatedly suffered from the calamity of fire.
The multitude sighed in lamentation and resentment,
finding no peace in their dwellings; consequently,
he issued an edict throughout the kingdom.
If there are those who are not careful,
they shall be moved to the Cold Forest (śītavana).
As for this "Cold Forest":
The place where corpses were discarded was commonly regarded by the people as an inauspicious site;
in an instant, a fire first broke out within the royal palace itself.
The king said to his ministers,
"The relocation is now complete.
He then ordered the crown prince to oversee the affairs of state.
He personally went out four or five *li* to the northwest of the thatched city and there established his residence.
At that time, the King of Vaiśālī...
He heard that King Bimbisāra was residing in the wilderness of the Cold Forest and had mobilized his troops,
intending to launch a surprise attack on him while he was unprepared.
The frontier guards reported this,
whereupon cities and towns were established;
because the King had previously resided here, it was so named.
It was called Rājagṛha;
the officials, retainers, scholars,
and commoners all moved their households there.
Some say it was established by King Ajātaśatru and reached the time of King Aśoka.
He moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra and bestowed Rājagṛha upon a brahmin.
Now, within this city,
there are no longer any commoners;
there are only Brahmins, numbering fewer than a thousand households.
Fourteen or fifteen *li* to the northeast of Mṛgadāva,
one reaches Gṛdhrakūṭa;
in the language of Tang, it means "Vulture Peak."
It is also called Vulture Peak;
situated on the southern slope of the northern range,
it rises up in solitary prominence.
Already inhabited by vultures,
it resembles a lofty terrace;
the azure sky and verdant foliage reflect one another.
The colors were distinguished by their intensity and subtlety.
Thus the Tathāgata governed the world for nearly fifty years.
He dwelt on this mountain for a long time and extensively expounded the sublime Dharma;
it was precisely at this location that he preached this sutra.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"He is always on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and in other various dwelling places."
When the Buddha was in the world,
King Bimbisāra, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, [went to visit him].
He mobilized a multitude of laborers to traverse from the mountain foot to the mountain peaks,
spanning valleys and scaling crags.
The stone steps were constructed by stacking stones;
they were over ten paces wide and five or six li in length.
Along the middle of the path stood two small stupas.
The first is called the "Lower Vehicle," by which the King proceeds on foot;
the second is called "Retreating from the Mundane."
He immediately excluded ordinary people and did not allow them to go with him.
At the summit of that mountain...
It is long from east to west and narrow from south to north.
It extends toward a precipice on its western side,
where there is currently a brick building.
Tall, wide, and marvelously constructed,
its doors open to the east;
it was here that the Tathāgata resided in the past to preach the Dharma.
Now, an image of the Buddha Preaching the Dharma has been fashioned,
its proportions equal to those of the Buddha’s own body.
[Recorded by] the Tang Dynasty Śramaṇa Xuanzang.
His secular surname was Chen,
and he was a native of Luoyang.
He left the household life at an early age.
From his youth, he possessed the capacity for wisdom and understanding;
he studied under renowned masters and thoroughly comprehended the true exegesis.
He considered that those who grasp at branches perceive only the minute,
while those who scoop from a stream recognize only the shallow;
thus they sacrifice their lives in remote frontiers.
He galloped through the crimson and white clouds toward the profound extremities;
at the beginning of the Zhenguan era,
he set out from his station and journeyed westward.
He traveled back and forth for seventeen years.
The scriptures and treatises he obtained are detailed in a separate record.
In that country of Central India,
he obtained a golden statue of the Buddha, modeled after the one at Vulture Peak Mountain in Magadha where the *Lotus Sūtra* was preached;
including its halo and pedestal, it stood three feet high.
His physical form is preeminent and surpasses all human craftsmanship;
one gazes up at him with reverence from the crown of one's head.
In reality, they increase ten-thousandfold and ten-thousandfold forever;
once they have come to rest,
they can be depicted and transcribed without end.
In the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty (423 CE),
the śramaṇa Bo Huigao of Waguan Monastery founded Lingjiu Monastery.
There was a śramaṇa named Shi Huìháo,
whose wisdom and insight were penetrating and acute,
and whose ingenious thought was peerless.
Within it, he fashioned a map of Vulture Peak;
its wondrous transformations were boundless,
appearing so lush and vibrant that one seemed to behold the reality itself.
The forms of the birds and beasts of its mountain forests,
and the appearances of the eight classes of devas and nāgas,
were unlike anything seen in previous generations.
From this point they first emerged;
after the niches were completed,
the entire nation came to behold them.
In later generations, niches were constructed,
all of which took the [original] model as their standard.
These niches were thirty-eight zhang deep from east to west.
It measures forty-four zhang and four chi from north to south.
In the first year of Tianxing, during the reign of Emperor Daizheng Tuoba Gui, the Taizu of the Later Wei dynasty.
He commissioned one painting of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain,
embellishing it with exquisite craftsmanship;
there was nothing that was not solemnly and fully equipped.
In the seventh year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty,
Lady Yin, the consort of the Governor of Jingzhou,
founded Dongqingyuan Temple.
In the fifteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Lady Xie constructed a Dharma Flower Altar within the temple.
In Moling County,
he established Fahua Temple. Later,
Zheng Qiong, the Duke of Gong and Grand Master of Ceremonies of the Northern Wei, [erected an inscription].
He founded Jingyu Monastery and constructed the Fahua Hall in the second year of the Xingning era of the Jin dynasty.
The śramaṇa Huili constructed a stone stūpa of Prabhūtaratna at Waguan Temple.
In the fifth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty,
Liu Fuai, a native of Pengcheng,
was in Jiankang.
He constructed Duobao Temple and also built one Duobao Pagoda in the first year of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty.
Hu Xiezhi, the Regional Inspector of Yuzhou,
constructed Fayin Temple on Mount Zhong.
Assisted by the palace attendant Xu Yan,
he constructed one stone Many-Treasures Stūpa.
[This was] the śramaṇa Facheng of Wuzhen Temple at Yushan in Lantian during the Tang dynasty.
Having left home at a young age,
he dwelt in the mountains, secluded from the world,
and recited this sutra.
Having recited it more than ten thousand times,
he constructed one Many-Jeweled Stūpa and one Lotus Sūtra Hall in accordance with the scripture.
One Hall of the Lotus Sutra;
one Lotus Sutra Altar;
the sutra is placed upon the altar.
He performed circumambulations and ritual repentances,
and further constructed a meditation chamber where he practiced meditative concentration.
There are numerous miraculous traces,
which are detailed in the subsequent tradition.
Xiao Jing, the Director of the National Academy of the Tang Dynasty, [recorded them].
A native of Lanling.
He was the great-grandson of the Emperor of Liang and the fifth son of Prince Gui of Liang.
When the Liang dynasty fell and she entered the Sui,
her elder sister became the Empress Dowager of Emperor Yang.
Having grown up in great nobility and prosperity, [she was]—
His family held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem.
During the Daye era,
he himself recited the Lotus Sūtra.
Then, following the scriptural text,
he constructed a stūpa of Prabhūtaratna, made of sandalwood.
The stupa was about three chi in height and contained a wooden image of Prabhūtaratna;
after several years, it had not yet been completed.
His elder brother’s son, Quan,
was at home;
he rose in the morning.
Suddenly, amidst the grass in the front courtyard,
he saw a sandalwood stupa;
beneath its canopy was a bronze Buddha image.
The craftsmanship was extraordinary;
the Brahmanic countenance was majestic and solemn,
and the pupils of the eyes were [vivid].
It was made of silver;
its center was black, radiant, and pure,
as if it were natural.
Quan was astonished;
he ran to inform Jing,
who looked at it and was filled with joyful surprise.
He took the canopy and returned;
when he tried placing it atop the Stūpa of Many Treasures,
it fit perfectly.
As for those made by the original craftsmen,
although the wood color was slightly different,
the shape of the stupa was even more exquisite.
He placed a Buddha image within the stupa,
constructing it in a manner consistent with its former appearance;
Jing was filled with joy and sighed in admiration.
He considered this to be a response moved by his own sincerity;
within the robes of the Buddha image,
there were more than a hundred śarīra relics.
The nun Jingnü and others,
being young, privately harbored doubts regarding the śarīra.
It could not be broken by hammering;
he then took thirty pieces and tested them upon a stone.
He struck it with an axe,
and the śarīra fragments scattered;
there was nothing at all that remained attached.
The woman searched for them on the ground and found only three or four pieces;
she could not see where the rest were.
Shortly thereafter, he became fearful and informed Jing.
Jing went into the stupa to look at it.
The śarīra relics remained exactly as they were before.
From that time on, Jing recited the Lotus Sūtra once every day.
This continued until his end.
In the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era,
his illness became critical.
Empress Xiao,
along with her younger brothers and nephews,
went to see him; Jing met them there.
He ordered incense to be lit for each of them,
and they then took their leave together;
he left behind only his younger brother, Song Gong Yu.
When the woman who had become a nun lit incense and recited the sutras for a short while,
[the image moved].
He said to that nun,
"I wish to depart;
[this is] Samantabhadra Bodhisattva."
"She has come to welcome me at the Eastern Courtyard;
you, Master, should go to welcome her.
The nun went as instructed to welcome her.
He did not return.
Jing said,
"This courtyard is impure."
"If he is unwilling to come,
I shall go to him.
You all should dwell well."
Having parted from Yu and the others,
he rose once more,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms.
He turned directly toward the west;
shortly thereafter, he passed away.
His final instructions were as follows:
He was carried alone in a single carriage;
he was shrouded in the garments worn during his lifetime,
and women were not permitted to escort him to the burial.
Do not offer meat in sacrifice.
The pit was just deep enough to submerge the coffin.
Both the court and the commoners marveled at his profound wisdom.
The members of the household received and practiced it.
In the past, the Great Being Samantabhadra possessed boundless supernatural powers.
Manifesting now as an Elephant King to bear witness to the Lotus Sutra—
this is perhaps the provisional response of a former Buddha,
or the transformative descent of one who dwells in the stage of the future Buddha.
It cannot be fathomed by those on the seventh stage,
nor can it be conceived of by those of the Two Vehicles. Indeed,
this is the most sublime and wondrous form-body.
Since the Way has been clarified,
its subtle and profound images have indeed moved the common people; this is truly inherent in the nature of things.
Following form to awaken to the spirit,
and tracing the traces to contemplate the source—
this is the aspect of the Manifestation of Joy.
This is truly the gateway and ford for inducing [beings] toward reality.
Empress Dowager Lü Zhao of the Song dynasty had planted [the seeds of merit] due to the vast kalpas of the past.
He stands as the peerless sovereign of the imperial house,
yet regards noble status as a mere dream and treasures as but worldly dust.
Sīlāditya (Si-lóng) sought to propagate the sublime transformation; in the fourth year of the Daming era,
he commissioned the monk Tánbiāo of Bǎimǎ Temple to produce a copy of the Dharmakāya.
He fashioned a single statue of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
riding upon a white elephant with six tusks, smooth and slender.
The seven limbs are level and full;
its construction is massive and grand,
and its casting is exquisite and rigorous.
Casting it like refined copper and smelting it with tin and silver,
the Bodhisattva’s features shine with the brilliance of purple-gold.
The elephant king shone with the form of white silver;
its brilliance was magnificent and dazzling,
appearing as if it were soaring upward.
It is truly a wondrous trace of the Buddha's work and the authentic model for stupas and temples;
yet his great vows remain inexhaustible.
He cultivated merit without weariness.
In the eighth year of the Daming era,
he further constructed Puxian Temple.
The marvel of its magnificence shall glorify its solemnity.
Shi Daojiong.
Fufeng was a man who loved the surging waves.
His original surname was Ma,
and his scholarly pursuits were pure and refined.
He gained renown in his youth.
When he first left the household life,
he became a disciple of Daoyi.
Jiong had long recited the Lotus Sutra,
relying solely on the sincerity of this practice.
In the ninth month of the second year of the Yuanjia era,
While in Luoyang,
he performed a Samantabhadra fast on behalf of others. Thereupon,
He cleansed the courtyard and its precincts,
purifying both the interior and exterior,
and installed an image of Samantabhadra.
With a heart of reverent solemnity,
about forty people, both monastics and laypersons,
had already been there for seven days.
Just as he was about to take his midday meal,
a man suddenly appeared riding a horse clad in trousers and a tunic,
entering and stopping before the hall.
He dismounted from his horse to pay homage to the Buddha.
Jiong remarked,
"Ordinary people do not show such exceptional courtesy."
This man mounted his horse and brandished his whip;
suddenly he vanished from sight,
and a brilliant red light was seen blazing across the entire sky.
After a long while, it vanished.
Three years later, in the twelfth month,
[it appeared] in the home of a layperson.
He further performed the Samantabhadra fast.
On the evening when it was about to conclude,
there were two śramaṇas.
His appearance was like that of an ordinary person;
he came directly to pay homage to the Buddha,
and those among the assembly took him to be a mediocre monk.
Not regarding him with much reverence,
he casually asked where he resided.
He replied:
He resided in the village ahead.
At that time, among the laypeople,
there was one named Zhang Dao.
Realizing there was something extraordinary about him,
he paid homage with a sincere heart.
The śramaṇa then went out the door.
After walking some tens of paces,
he suddenly flew up into the air and soared straight toward the heavens.
He followed the monk's gaze with his eyes.
No longer knowing where to go,
he later traveled south with four fellow students to Yangdu,
where they observed the local customs and social transformations.
At night they crossed the river on ice;
midway through, the ice broke,
and three men drowned.
Jiong again returned his sincerity to Avalokiteśvara,
whereupon he felt as if something were supporting him from beneath his feet;
he further saw a red light before him.
Riding upon the light, he reached the shore and established his capital;
he resided at Nanjian Temple.
He constantly took the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* as his practice.
Once, during the middle of the night, while he had entered into meditation,
he suddenly saw four men driving a carriage arrive at his room.
He called out to those on the upper carriage, who suddenly and without realizing it found themselves at Junling Shenqiao.
There he saw a man seated upon a *huchuang* (Hindu-style chair) by the roadside,
with several hundred attendants waiting for him.
Seeing this, [Fajiong] started in alarm and said,
"I am but a practitioner of seated meditation.
Thereupon, the man addressed his attendants, saying:
"It was merely to direct him toward the place so that he might know it;
why did you suddenly trouble yourself to humble the Dharma Master?
Thereupon, [he said]:
Having performed prostrations and taken leave,
he had a messenger escort him back to the monastery,
where he knocked on the gate.
After a long while, it finally opened.
Upon entering the monastery, he found that his room was still closed;
the assembly could not fathom why this was so.
In the twentieth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty,
Yi Qing, the Prince of Kang of Linchuan,
took him along to Guangling.
Finally, there was Shi Sengbao,
a native of Jingzhao.
In his youth, he resided at Guanzhong and received instruction from Master Kumārajīva.
During the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he...
Traveling north,
he gradually entered the Huangshan Monastery,
where he established a seven-day-and-three-night Pu-xian (Samantabhadra) vegetarian retreat.
When the repentance ceremony reached the seventeenth day,
a white crane flew in and alighted before the seat of Samantabhadra.
They departed after the incense had been offered at midday.
On the twenty-first day,
there were again four people dressed in yellow robes.
After circumambulating the stupa several times,
he suddenly vanished.
*The Biography of the Propagation of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll One.
*The Record of the Propagation and Praise of the Lotus Sūtra*, Scroll Two, compiled by the Śramaṇa Huixiang of Langu Valley. Section Two:

Translations. Regarding the authenticity of the translated scriptures, there are fourteen individuals in total: ten authentic, four spurious, and two who were involved in the discourse on translation.
The *Fahua Sanmei Jing* (Lotus Samādhi Sūtra) in six fascicles by the foreign Indian Śramaṇa Zheng Wuweī; also one version with the character "Zheng" (Correct) added.

The *Zhengfahua Jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra) in ten fascicles by the Dunhuang Śramaṇa Zhu Fahu of the Jin dynasty; also separately issued as the *Pumenpin Jing* (Universal Gate Chapter) and the *Guangshiyin Jing* (Avalokiteśvara Sūtra).
The *Pumenpin Jing* by the Śramaṇa Hachi from the Western Regions of the Eastern Jin dynasty. The [Pumenpin] by the Śramaṇa Zhidao Gen of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The Vaipulya *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in five fascicles; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one work in seven fascicles, translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Kumārajīva during the pseudo-Qin;
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhìyán of Jǐngzhōu during the Song;

the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, translated by Jìngshēng, younger brother of the King of Hexi of Northern Liáng during the Song; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* by the Śramaṇa Fǎxiàn of Shànglín Monastery during the Qi.
The *Devadatta-parivarta* (Chapter on Devadatta), translated by the Xiyu monk Shi Dezhi of the Sui dynasty;

the *Samantamukha-parivarta* (Universal Gateway Chapter) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, consisting of re-chanted verses, translated by the Xiyu monk Shi Fami of the Tang dynasty; the *Tārakopama-parivarta* (Chapter on the Simile of the Medicinal Herbs) with five additional sheets of various dhāraṇīs, all differing from the Qi edition;
and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-uddhṛta-dharma* (Extracted Dharma of the Lotus Sutra), compiled by Xiao Ziliang, Prince Jingling of the Qi dynasty.

*Huāyào wáng jīng* (Sutra of the Flower-Medicine King), one fascicle; translated by Jiang Mi, a female disciple of the Great Master of Liang. *Fǎhuá jīng* (Lotus Sutra), one fascicle. The above two entries are not authentic scriptures.

Among the ancient and old catalogs, there are two lost-translator scriptures: *Fǎhuá guāngruì púsà xiànshòu jīng* (The Lotus Light-Auspicious Bodhisattva Manifests Longevity Sutra) with annotations by Fei Changfang of the Sui dynasty; and the apocryphal scriptures *Miaofa lianhua duoliang tiandi jing* (The Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sutra on Measuring Heaven and Earth) and *Miaofa lianhua tiandi biànyì jing* (The Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sutra on the Transformations of Heaven and Earth). The above two entries are suspected of being apocryphal.

*The Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra* in two fascicles by the Śramaṇa Daohi of the Western Regions during the Later Wei; *The Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra* in one fascicle by the Śramaṇa Baoyi of Central India during the Later Wei; and *The Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Lotus Flower* in six fascicles—one version includes the character "zheng" (correct). The above.
The foreign śramaṇa Zhiqiangliangjie—
whose name means "Correct Fearlessness" in the Wei language—
arrived in the seventh month of the first year of the Shigangan era of Emperor Gaoguangqinggong of the Wei dynasty.
Translated at Jiaozhou;
the śramaṇa Daoxin recorded it in writing.
This is how it appears in the separate extensive catalog of scriptures.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in ten fascicles.
Translated by the śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa (translated here as Fǎhù).
His ancestors were people of the Yuezhi;
his original surname was Zhi,
and his family had resided for generations in Dunhuang Commandery.
At the age of eight, he left home to become a monk.
He served the foreign śramaṇa Zhu Gaosuo as his teacher and recited ten thousand words of scripture daily.
He could master anything upon a single glance;
by nature he was pure and noble,
and his conduct was refined and austere.
He was earnest in his resolve and fond of learning;
he traveled ten thousand *li* to seek out a teacher.
For this reason:
He had extensively studied the Six Classics and allowed his mind to roam through the Seven Canons; yet,
regarding worldly affairs and the slanders or praises thereof—
I have never harbored such a thought.
At that time, during the reign of Emperor Wu of Jin,
there were images in temples and monasteries.
Although the capital was held in high esteem, the profound treasury of the Vaipulya sutras lay beyond the Pamir Mountains; thereupon,
Saṃghavarman sighed with resolve and roused his indignation,
vowing to propagate the Great Way.
He then followed his master to the Western Regions,
traveling through various kingdoms; there,
he encountered the diverse languages of foreign lands.
There are thirty-six kinds;
calligraphy is likewise.
He protected [the teachings] by studying them all thoroughly.
He thoroughly mastered glosses and explanations;
there were no phonetics, meanings,
or character forms that he did not fully comprehend.
He then took a great number of Sanskrit scriptures and returned to China,
traveling from Dunhuang to Chang’an.
Along the way, he acted as a translator,
transcribing [the texts] into the language of Jin.
